title: USPS now offers official ZIP Code boundary polygons
titleZh: USPS now offers official ZIP Code boundary polygons
author: munro
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: USPS® ZIP Code Boundaries is a national ZIP Code™ map utilizing USPS delivery address and location information to ensure accurate boundaries. Temporal fluctuation is based on changing delivery distribution for new or changed delivery locations. Many industries, such as mapping, mailing, marketing, insurance, real estate, logistics, navigation, and transportation can benefit from access to the ZIP Code boundary data.

As the ground truth for ZIP Code boundaries, users can incorporate these polygons as joint features or correct existing ZIP Code data as changes are made. As a tool for organizing and displaying demographic data, ZIP Codes serve as a support structure for real estate and insurance industries. ZIP Codes can serve as a proxy for the delivery location groupings for optimized routing.

comments.author: SwellJoe
comments.textRawHtml: Dang, the prices are crazy. $10k for the lowest tier? I expect federal data to be free. Most federal data related to stuff like regulation (e.g. FCC spectrum use coverage maps), maps for federally-managed lands, etc. is free. And, it should be free. It's a core part of accountability and transparency. Historically there was a copying cost (having a human print physical copies on paper or CD/DVD/tape), which is understandable, but now that the incremental cost of each new copy approaches $0, that's what it should cost users of the data.

children.author: nonethewiser
children.textRawHtml:
>USPS is in a strange boat where a lot of people insist that it must be profitable, much like UPS or Fedex

This isn't really accurate. USPS had a break even (not profitability) legal mandate since 1970-2006. They would adjust prices each year to hit break even. And that's what happened - they roughly broke even each year.

After a 2006 with broad bipartisan support, the UPS was able to make a profit (not just break even) but a price cap was added (to be reviewed every 10 years). They couldn't raise costs beyond inflation. A stamp to send to anywhere in the USA - anywhere (Alaska, Guam, etc.) - currently costs 82 cent. The postal union is against this, usps management is against this, and business mailers are for it. Dont you love all the ads USPS delivers you?

They have not been break even since 2007. They currently lose about $9B/year with $2.7BM being controllable and the rest largely being pensions, retiree health plans, and workers comp charges. Their core business (mail) has been declining for 20 years and no end is in sight. In 2020 they loosened the cap a bit (allowing USPS to raise prices). Business mailers tried to sue them but lost.

So this attitude that they should just lose a bunch of money and be backstopped by the taxpayer, when mail is less critical than ever, is an recent idea and is aligned with business mailer lobbying interests. It seems obvious to me that they should just go back to the break even mandate.

children.author: hammock
children.textRawHtml:
>The postal union is against this, usps management is against this, and business mailers are for it

I was confused by this until I realized you are missing some logical steps in your (accurate) argument.

The 2006 law took away the safety net (ie the ability to charge whatever is needed to break even).

The “you can now make a profit” rule actually made it HARDER since it came with a price cap.

It told the USPS: You can keep any profits you make, but you cannot raise prices above the rate of inflation to get them.

This forced the USPS to absorb rising costs through internal efficiency rather than passing the bill to mailers

children.author: wahern
children.textRawHtml:
I'm guessing that was what the lobbyists intended. Nominally the law permitted a profit, and that's how it was sold, but it was structured as a bulk mailer subsidy. Strategic discourse subterfuge.

Also, FWIW, AFAIK the lions share of the USPS deficit is for funding healthcare benefits. Healthcare costs are rising much faster than inflation, and because they're finding future obligations that additional inflationary margin is a killer. Pension obligations are now under control. Of course, fully funding your benefit obligations is the right thing to do, but public agencies have been making promises they can't keep and the USPS is a rarity in being forced to properly fund them rather than kick the can down the road. It's unfair in one sense, but perfectly fair in another.

A big thing they could do for costs is reduce mail delivery to the final destination to once or twice a week. They would need anywhere from 1/2 to 1/5 the number of delivery drivers and vehicles that they have today.

The vast majority of first-class and bulk-rate mail is not anything can't wait a few days. For truly urgent deliveries, use a courier service or pay a higher postage that covers the expenses of that.

children.author: its_ethan
children.textRawHtml:
> They would need anywhere from 1/2 to 1/5 the number of delivery drivers and vehicles that they have today

And that's why it (unfortunately) won't happen lol the USPS is as much of a jobs program as it is an actual mail delivery service.

As the guy above you pointed out, the postal workers union exists, and would fight this tooth and nail. Additionally, without legislation forcing it, management at USPS doesn't really have any incentive or ability to fire 1/2 to 4/5ths of their workers, those saved tax dollars don't really matter to them.

As much as I agree it could be made much more efficient, doing so would probably be very unpopular politically. For as often as people have negative experiences with the USPS, no one wants to see their friendly neighborhood post carrier (who walks around in a fun outfit dropping off letters and packages to them) get canned.

children.author: toomuchtodo
children.textRawHtml:
That’s $2B less than the first six days of the Iran war ($11B). We could just cut a check each year from the general fund. It’s a paperwork issue. The fact that we can spend $100B+ on an illegitimate conflict on a whim while costs like this are bikeshedded over boggles my mind.

US Military costs ~$1T/year and the Pentagon hasn’t passed an audit in the last eight years, comparatively, but not a lot of similar complaints of that waste versus pensions for workers operating and serving a national public service agency.

https://www.militarytimes.com/news/pentagon-congress/2025/12...

Electrifying the USPS light vehicle fleet is expected to generate up to $4.3B in lifetime savings over the fleet lifecycle, similarly.

children.author: toomuchtodo
children.textRawHtml:
Additional follow on thought:

USPS and the US military are both, at their heart, logistics engines and systems, and both should be valued as such. "The whole is more than the sum of its parts." If you do not maintain and treat said systems with respect, the capability will not be ready when you need it, or will not contribute to the ongoing success of the jurisdiction in which it operates. The only difference between the two is that the US military happens to fight wars with what its logistics operation it provides itself.

The unsung role of logistics in the US military - https://news.mit.edu/2025/unsung-role-logistics-us-military-... - November 25, 2025

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_logistics
